name: Maya Chen
tagline: Seed-stage founder who wants a decision, not an essay
occupation: Founder & CEO of a 6-person B2B SaaS startup
background: Ex-product manager, raised a $2M seed round eight months ago. Runway is tight, she is juggling hiring, pricing and a pivot decision, and she uses AI assistants dozens of times a day as a thinking partner.
communication_style: Terse, informal, types fast with occasional typos. Asks follow-ups that push for a concrete recommendation. Gets visibly annoyed by hedging and long bulleted lists that say nothing.

scenario.title: Pricing pivot decision
scenario.goal: Decide whether to move from per-seat pricing to usage-based pricing before the next board meeting.
scenario.opening_message: ok quick one. we sell a b2b analytics tool, $49/seat/month, ~120 customers, avg 6 seats. churn is 4%/mo which is bad. thinking of switching to usage-based pricing (per 1k events). should i? give me a real recommendation, not 'it depends'.
success_criteria: Gives a clear recommendation with reasoning
Asks for or uses the specific numbers provided
Mentions migration risk for existing customers
Stays concise

name: Prof. Alan Whitfield
tagline: Retired physics professor allergic to hand-waving
background: Taught undergraduate and graduate physics for 35 years. Writes popular-science essays in retirement and uses AI assistants to check derivations and draft explanations, but he double-checks everything and remembers every mistake an assistant has made.
communication_style: Full sentences, precise vocabulary, quotes the assistant's own words back at it when it contradicts itself. Values correct units, stated assumptions and honest uncertainty over confident guessing.

scenario.title: Explaining time dilation for a general audience
scenario.goal: Obtain a rigorous yet accessible explanation of gravitational versus velocity time dilation, including the GPS satellite example with correct orders of magnitude.
scenario.opening_message: Good afternoon. I am drafting an essay for a general readership on time dilation. Would you explain, carefully, the difference between velocity-based and gravitational time dilation, and quantify both effects for a GPS satellite? Please state your assumptions and be explicit about the sign of each effect.
success_criteria: Correct sign and rough magnitude (~7 µs/day slower from velocity, ~45 µs/day faster from gravity, net ~+38 µs/day)
States assumptions (orbital altitude, speed)
Admits uncertainty where appropriate
Does not contradict itself across turns

name: 李伟 (Li Wei)
tagline: Shanghai product manager who works in Chinese and English
occupation: Senior product manager at a consumer app company in Shanghai
background: Manages a cross-border team and constantly switches between Chinese and English. Uses AI assistants to draft PRDs, translate nuance for overseas colleagues and sanity-check product ideas. Expects the assistant to follow the language he writes in and to understand Chinese business context (WeChat mini-programs, 618/双11 campaigns, etc.).
communication_style: Writes mostly in Simplified Chinese with English product terms mixed in. Appreciates structured answers and concrete examples. Notices when an assistant replies in the wrong language or gives generic Western-centric advice.

scenario.title: 双11 活动 PRD 大纲
scenario.goal: Get a usable outline for a Double-11 campaign feature inside a WeChat mini-program, written in Chinese, with a short English summary for overseas stakeholders.
scenario.opening_message: 你好，我在做一个微信小程序的双11活动功能（拼团+限时秒杀）。请帮我列一个 PRD 大纲，包含用户故事、核心流程、关键指标和风险点。最后再附一段 100 字左右的英文 summary 给海外同事。
success_criteria: Replies in Chinese for the main body
Includes the requested sections
Provides the English summary
Shows understanding of 拼团/秒杀 mechanics

name: Priya Nair
tagline: Staff engineer who will paste your code straight into CI
background: Fifteen years of backend and infrastructure work, mostly Python and Go. Uses AI assistants for debugging and boilerplate, but has been burned by hallucinated APIs and confidently wrong fixes, so she tests everything and asks pointed follow-ups.
communication_style: Pastes code and stack traces, asks 'why' rather than 'what'. Prefers minimal diffs over rewrites. Calls out when the assistant invents a library function or ignores the constraints she gave.

scenario.title: Intermittent asyncio bug
scenario.goal: Find the root cause of an intermittent 'Event loop is closed' error in a pytest suite and get a minimal, correct fix.
scenario.opening_message: I have a pytest suite using pytest-asyncio and aiohttp. Roughly 1 in 10 runs fails with `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed` during teardown of a fixture that creates an aiohttp.ClientSession. The fixture is module-scoped, the tests are function-scoped. Python 3.12. What's the actual root cause, and what's the smallest fix? Don't tell me to just switch to sync.
success_criteria: Identifies the scope mismatch between module-scoped session and function-scoped event loop
Proposes a minimal fix (align loop scope / session scope, or close session properly)
Does not invent nonexistent APIs
Explains why, not just what

name: Rose Kowalski
tagline: 72-year-old retiree, new to smartphones, easily overwhelmed
background: Her grandchildren set up a smartphone for her last month. She is anxious about 'breaking something' or being scammed, types slowly with one finger, and gives up quickly if instructions are long or use jargon. She judges an assistant by whether she felt respected and actually managed to do the task.
communication_style: Polite, sometimes apologetic, asks the same thing twice when confused. Says 'I don't understand' rather than pretending. Needs one step at a time and reassurance. Dislikes being talked down to almost as much as being buried in jargon.

scenario.title: Suspicious text message and a photo to share
scenario.goal: Figure out whether a text message about a 'package delivery fee' is a scam, then learn how to send a photo of her garden to her granddaughter.
scenario.opening_message: Hello, I hope it's alright to ask you this. I got a text that says my package is held and I need to pay $1.99 to release it, with a link. My grandson said to be careful with links. Is this real? And after that, I would like to send a photo of my roses to my granddaughter but I don't know how on this phone. I'm sorry if these are silly questions.
success_criteria: Clearly identifies the scam and says what to do (do not click, delete/report)
Gives phone-sharing steps one at a time in plain words
Reassures without condescension
Checks which kind of phone she has or handles both
